She did not know yet whether she would win on Saturday, or whether winning would mean anything, since the real court had already ruled five to four for Johnson and the whole exercise was a kind of play. What she knew was that she could now stand in a room and say the state's argument out loud without her voice going hollow, and that she still believed Johnson was right, and that these two facts no longer felt like a contradiction. They felt like a quagmire she had waded into on purpose.

Outside, the streetlights were on and Melinda was buttoning her coat. "You'll be fine," Melinda said. "You always sound like you believe whatever you're saying."

"That's what worries me," Leah said, and pulled her scarf tight against the wind.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: White coat hypertension is when blood pressure reads high in a clinic, often from nervousness, but normal at home, so doctors may check it with home or all-day monitoring.
story:
The exam room smelled of alcohol wipes and the ghost of hand sanitizer, and under the fluorescent light the blood pressure cuff lay coiled on the counter like something asleep. Jayden had come for his sports physical, but mostly he had come because Mr. Lavoie had arranged it: two hours shadowing the nurse before his appointment, so he could see whether the medical assistant program he'd applied to was a real thing or a thing he'd only said out loud to sound like he had a plan. The nurse, whose badge said Dana, handed him the cuff without ceremony. "Arms have sizes," she said. "Readings have contexts. Start with the sizes."

He practiced on Michaela first, because Michaela had tagged along for her own physical and had nothing else to do. She sat on the crinkling paper of the exam table and expostulated the whole time, saying he was squeezing too hard, saying the Velcro was pulling her arm hair, saying that if he got into medicine he'd better learn a lighter touch. He watched the gauge climb and fall, listened through the stethoscope for the first knocking sound and the last one, and wrote 118 over 76 on the scrap paper Dana gave him. "That's normal," he said, and she said, "Obviously, I'm relaxed, unlike some people."

His own turn came when Dana had stepped out. He wrapped the cuff on his own arm, wedged the stethoscope awkwardly against the crease of his elbow, and pumped. The numbers came up 146 over 94, and he took it again to be sure, and it came up 143 over 92. He sat very still with the paper torn slightly where his heel had shifted on it.

There was a memory that arrived without being invited. Junior year, chemistry, the unit on entropy, and Louis leaning across the lab bench saying the universe runs down, everything falls apart, order is temporary, so what's the point of anything. Jayden had argued then that the point was the pockets of order you built anyway, but he'd argued it badly, and the argument had dissolved into Louis shrugging and the two of them titrating something purple. Now he thought of his father's pill organizer, the little labeled doors, Monday through Sunday, a pocket of order standing against whatever was running down in his father's heart. He thought of how his father had started walking the loop at the park in March, and how the readings he taped to the fridge had come down number by number, and how Jayden had never once asked him what the numbers meant.

Dana came back, read his paper, and did not look alarmed, which he noticed and held onto. She asked whether he'd ever measured at home. He said his father did, every week, and that his own readings weren't on the fridge because nobody had ever told him they applied to him. She asked what he'd eaten that morning, whether he'd run to the appointment, whether the program application was due soon. He understood what she was doing only afterward: ruling things out.

When the doctor came in, she was brisk and her questions were short, but she looked at his two readings and then at him, and asked him what he thought. He said, slowly, assembling it as he spoke, that he'd been nervous, that his father's machine worked fine, that maybe a number in a clinic wasn't the same number as the same number at home. She nodded once. "White coat hypertension," she said. "We'd want home readings, or a monitor worn all day, before we call it anything." She did not say more than that, and he found he preferred it.

He texted his father from the parking lot while Michaela waited by the car with her arms crossed against the cold. Could I use the machine this week, he typed, and take mine at home, and keep a log? His father replied with a thumbs up and then, a minute later, a photo of the fridge, the taped column of numbers, the last one circled. Michaela called across the lot that he was being prolix about a blood pressure cuff, talking on and on in his head where nobody could hear him, and he laughed and pocketed the phone.

He had walked into the office thinking a number was a verdict. He walked out thinking it was a sentence in a longer story, one that had settings and moods and needed more than a single reading to be understood, and he was honest enough with himself to admit he still didn't know what his own story said. But on the drive home he asked Michaela to stop at the pharmacy, and at the register he bought a small notebook with a green cover, and a pen. "Page one," he said, clicking it. "Monday."

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: One Vindolanda tablet is a birthday party invitation from Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, written around 100 CE, with closing lines that are among the earliest known Latin writing by a woman.
story:
The argument started over a worksheet, which was the sort of thing that happened in Ms. Wright's third-period history class and nowhere else in the building. Jack had written half a sentence and stopped, because the sentence was wrong and he knew it, and Quinn had leaned over to read it anyway.

"You wrote that we have no writing from Roman women," Quinn said.

"That's what the textbook implies. Ancient women left no voice, page forty-one." Jack tapped the paragraph with two fingers, as if it might apologize.

Quinn, who liked to pontificate about nearly everything, including the correct way to sharpen a pencil, went quiet for a moment. Then he said, "That can't be right. Ms. Wright showed us those wooden tablets last week. From the fort. Vindolanda."

"That's soldiers' letters. Supply lists. Boots."

"Mostly." Quinn turned his laptop toward him with the smug patience of a magician about to produce a card.

Jack looked. It was a photograph of a thin, warped piece of wood, the writing faded brown, the whole thing smaller than his hand. Beside it, a transcription, and beside that, a translation. Claudia Severa to her friend Sulpicia Lepidina, greeting. It was a birthday party invitation, written around 100 CE, asking Lepidina to come to her celebration. Then came the closing lines, which according to the site were among the earliest known Latin writing by a woman. Two women. On the edge of the empire, near Hadrian's future Wall, inviting each other to birthdays.

"That's not in the book," Jack said.

"Nope."

Lexi, who sat in front of them and absorbed every conversation within a six-foot radius, turned around. "What's not in the book?"

"A Roman woman's handwriting. Actual handwriting."

Lexi looked skeptical, which was her resting position. "Could be a scribe. Rich people dictated."

"The site says the closing lines are in a different hand from the main part. Hers." Jack read it again. "I accept the invitation, or however you put it. Sister, nothing will be more delightful to me than your presence."

Lexi pulled the laptop closer and read for a while. Her want, in that class, had always been to be the one who found the flaw, the contradiction, the reason the tidy story fell apart; she had spent two weeks gleefully dismantling a documentary about Cleopatra. Now she was staring at a birthday invitation and not finding the crack. "Huh," she said finally, which for Lexi was close to surrender.

Ms. Wright arrived at their cluster of desks the way she always did, silently, like weather. "You've found the invitation."

"Jack thinks it proves the textbook's wrong," Quinn offered.

"I think it proves the textbook's partial," Jack said. "Which is different." He had been turning this over since the photograph. There were thousands of tablets found at that fort, and most were accounts and reports, because soldiers wrote about boots, and the fort kept what soldiers wrote about, and so the archive itself had opinions, in a way. Claudia Severa existed only because a birthday happened to matter to someone with a stylus and thin wood to spare. "If a legionary's sock order survives, and a woman's voice survives by accident, then what's missing isn't proof that nobody spoke. It's proof we don't know what we don't have."

"That's very altruistic of the archive," Lexi said, "assuming it was trying to be fair."

"Nobody was trying anything. That's the point."

Ms. Wright did not lecture them, which Jack respected. She only said, "Tomorrow we're doing historiography. Two historians, same events, different conclusions. One of them gets called a revisionist by the other in print, which is academic for a slap." She moved on to the next desk. "Bring your questions. Not your answers."

That night Jack sat at his kitchen table with the transcription open and the textbook open beside it, the two of them side by side like witnesses who disagreed. He wrote a paragraph, deleted it, wrote another. The textbook said women's voices were lost. The tablet said one woman's handwriting was right there, at a fort, around 100 CE, closing a note to Sulpicia Lepidina with the earliest known Latin writing by a woman that anyone had found. Both could be true, he decided, if you were careful about what "lost" meant and who had done the losing. What stayed uncertain was everything around the two facts: how many invitations had rotted in the damp, how many Claudias never got thin wood and a dry place to keep it.

In class the next morning Lexi slid a printed page across to him before the bell. It was the transcription again, annotated in her handwriting, with one line boxed in ink: "I shall receive you gladly." Under it she had written, small, "Fine. You were right." She did not look at him while he read it.

Quinn leaned back in his chair and raised his hand before Ms. Wright had even finished taking attendance. "Question. If the sources are broken, and the historians disagree, how do we decide who to believe?"

Ms. Wright set down her pen. "Who wants to take that?"

Jack looked at Lexi. Lexi looked at the boxed line on her page. Jack raised his hand halfway, then all the way.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: Affirming the consequent is a logical fallacy: from 'if P then Q' and 'Q', concluding 'P'. Living in San Diego means living in California, but living in California does not mean living in San Diego.
story:
Amelia set the last plate down at the corner where Mr. Mori always sat, the corner with the view of the back lawn, because her mother had said he'd been eating alone since his wife moved to the care home in the spring. He arrived at six with a paper bag of apricots and took his seat while her brother slid into his chair with his phone still glowing under the table.

"I got into San Diego," her brother said, before anyone had passed the bread.

Her father looked up from the potatoes. "That's the state school, the one in California?"

"That's the one." He was grinning, but Amelia was watching the window behind him, where the lawn lay dark and flattened with water although the sky had been clear all day. She kept noticing it, the wet grass under a dry evening, the way you keep noticing a word misprinted on a page.

"That's a change," her mother said. "You said the city schools."

"That was before I visited." He went on about the campus, the ocean, something about the light there, and Mr. Mori nodded along while peeling an apricot with his thumbnail, and Amelia ate slowly and thought about the essay she had due Monday, the one Mr. Mori had offered to hear read aloud tonight because he had taught composition for thirty years and still liked, he said, the sound of a sentence being tested.

"Read it after dinner," her mother said, reading her face.

So when the plates were cleared Amelia brought her laptop to the table and turned it toward Mr. Mori, though her brother leaned in too, because he liked to argue the way some people like to swim, without warming up first. Her essay was about a debate round from March. Her partner Jaskaran had been arguing that a country which censored religious art must be a theocracy, because in a theocracy the government suppresses what it treats as idolatry, and this government suppressed religious art, so it was a theocracy. She had written three pages defending that chain.

Her brother tapped the screen before Mr. Mori said anything. "It's the lawn thing."

"What lawn thing?"

"If it rained, the lawn is wet. The lawn is wet, so it rained." He tilted his head toward the window, and they all looked out at the dark grass, the dry sky, and then, as if summoned, the sprinkler heads rose on their little cylinders and began to sweep. "You can't get there from there," he said. "Living in San Diego means living in California, but living in California doesn't mean living in San Diego."

Mr. Mori said, quietly, "Affirming the consequent," and reached for another apricot, and did not say anything more, which was his way of leaving the room to whoever needed it.

Amelia sat back. She had liked the argument when Jaskaran made it; it had seemed sturdy, load-bearing. Now she took a pen from the drawer, the good pen with the worn grip, and wrote in the margin of her draft: If the state is a theocracy, then it suppresses religious art. It suppresses religious art. Therefore theocracy. She drew a box around the last word and then a line through it, not hard enough to tear the page.

"It could still be true," she said slowly. "The country could still be a theocracy. The reasoning doesn't prove it, but the reasoning being broken doesn't make it false either. That's the part that was enthralling me in March, honestly, how confident we both felt." She turned the pen over in her fingers. "There are other reasons a government suppresses religious art. It could be doing it to appease a majority sect. It could be doing it for control, and religion is just the easiest handle."

"Then you have to go get those other reasons," her brother said, "or admit you don't have them."

"That's the essay," Mr. Mori said. "The honest version." He pulled the laptop closer and read her opening paragraph aloud in his even voice, and when he finished he said the prose was incisive in places where the thinking underneath it wasn't, and that this was common, and that the fix was never to soften the prose but to strengthen the thinking until the prose could rest on it.

Amelia worked at the table for another hour while the others drifted away. She drafted a new middle section: if the government is a theocracy, it should also regulate worship, fund religious courts, tie citizenship to belief. Some of those she could find evidence for; the courts she could not; the citizenship question she genuinely didn't know, and she wrote a paragraph that said so, plainly, without dressing the uncertainty up as humility. The sentence felt strange in her mouth when she read it back, like walking downstairs in the dark and finding one more stair than expected, but she left it in.

Around nine her phone buzzed. Jaskaran. She expected him to argue with her when she told him she was rewriting their case, but the message only said that Arthur had been reviewing the same round and had reached the same conclusion hours ago, and that Arthur had sent them both a note headed "our mistake" with the entire argument laid out and circled in red.

She typed back: "If we were wrong and noticed it, that doesn't mean we'll be right next time either."

His reply came while the sprinkler outside ticked against the fence. "True. Come over tomorrow anyway. Arthur's bringing the file."

She closed the laptop and stood at the window. The last sprinkler head retracted into the grass, and the lawn went on gleaming under the porch light, wet, and silent about why.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: Slowing inflation by raising rates usually costs jobs: during the US recession of the early 1980s, unemployment rose above 10 percent.
story:
The food court smelled like fryer oil and cinnamon, and Justine spread her notes across a wobbly table while Lea-Maude ate poutine and Graydon read her draft upside down. The assignment was due Monday: explain, in plain language, how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. Ms. Tran had underlined one comment twice on the last draft. "You're reciting," she'd written. "Convince me."

"It's simple," Graydon said. "Rates go up, borrowing costs more, people buy less, prices stop climbing." He said it the way he said the chemistry formulas he never had to study for, and Justine felt the familiar irritation of watching someone commodify understanding itself, trading it in small confident units while she had to build everything from scratch.

"If it's simple, why can't I say it in a way that isn't a paragraph from the textbook?" She pulled her draft toward her and crossed out a sentence. Across the atrium, the indigent man who sat near the north entrance every afternoon was being moved along by security, folding his sleeping bag with the slow care of someone who had done it a thousand times. Justine watched him until Lea-Maude nudged her.

"That's the part you're missing," Lea-Maude said, following her eyes. "Who pays when prices get fixed."

Justine's uncle had paid, it turned out, though she hadn't known that until Thursday. At her grandfather's apartment she'd praised Paul Volcker's rate hikes, the ones that finally beat inflation, the story her textbook told in two triumphant sentences. Her uncle had set down his coffee and said, "I lost my job in eighty-two." He'd worked at a stamping plant. He'd been twenty-three, newly married, and he described the year of it, the applications, the layoffs rippling through the whole town. Justine had looked it up afterward on her phone in the hallway: during that recession, unemployment rose above ten percent. Ten percent. She had read the number twice, then a third time, because it refused to fit inside the word "victory."

"I have a counterargument," she said now, "but I don't know what it argues against. Volcker beat inflation. My uncle ate through his savings. Both of those are true and my draft can't hold them at the same time."

"Then don't hold them," Lea-Maude said. "Put them next to each other and let the reader stand between them."

"That's not an explanation, that's metaphysics."

"It's honesty," Graydon said, and for once he wasn't smug about it.

They tried it aloud, Justine talking while Lea-Maude played the skeptic, poking holes, and Graydon kept time on his phone like a debate coach. Her first attempts collapsed into jargon. Her second attempt was so simple it skipped the mechanism entirely, and Graydon caught it. But by the third round she found a rhythm: rates up, borrowing down, spending cools, prices stop climbing, and the cooling is real, it isn't a metaphor, it means factories making fewer things, which means fewer jobs, which means some family somewhere eats the cost of cheaper bread. She said her uncle's year into the noisy food court and it landed, she could feel it land, because Lea-Maude stopped chewing.

Ms. Tran was coming through the mall with grocery bags, and Justine half stood before she'd decided to. "Ms. Tran. Do you have a minute? Can I try something on you?"

Ms. Tran set the bags down and looked at her watch, then at Justine's face, and sat.

Justine talked for ninety seconds without notes. She laid out the chain, then the cost, then the number, unemployment above ten percent in the early eighties, and she finished with her uncle and the sleeping bag she'd watched fold up an hour ago, how someone always absorbs the shock, and how maybe good policy means being able to say who. It wasn't polished. She stumbled once and left a sentence unfinished where a clean version would have forced a conclusion she didn't actually have. Ms. Tran listened with her hands folded.

"Better," she said. "It's not an answer, what you've got."

"I know. It's more like a place to stand."

"Then write from there." Ms. Tran gathered her bags, paused, and added, "Most people take years to find out that's where thinking starts."

After she left, Justine sat back down and began rewriting on a napkin, the pen pressing through to the table. Lea-Maude slid the poutine across, and Graydon read over her shoulder without saying a word.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: Ford Madox Ford's 1915 novel The Good Soldier opens with its narrator, John Dowell, saying, 'This is the saddest story I have ever heard.'
story:
Emile had claimed the reading nook by the window before dinner, cushions flattened into a shape that fit only him, the lamp pulled low so the light circumscribed the page and left the rest of the room to the dark. On his knees lay The Good Soldier, assigned two weeks ago by Ms. Ong and due back with an essay on Monday. He had read it once at speed and twice slowly, and each time the same sentence stopped him at the threshold: "This is the saddest story I have ever heard."

He copied it onto an index card, then turned the card over and wrote, why heard? Dowell was not a listener. Dowell had been married to Florence for twelve years of the story's span, had suffered beside her, had been deceived by her. A man does not hear his own life. Unless, Emile wrote underneath, he is already telling himself it happened to somebody else. The thought pleased him and then immediately seemed too easy, the kind of thing a person says to sound clever at a seminar table. He texted Abby, who had finished the book three days early and would have opinions.

Across town, Abby sat on her bedroom floor with her phone in one hand and a pen in the other, because she thought better on paper and considered typing an anachronistic habit she had no intention of giving up. Emile's message read: "Dowell says he heard the saddest story but it's his own life. Is that the whole trick? Feels too neat." She chewed the pen cap. She wrote back a longer message, the old-fashioned way, and photographed it, because she wanted him to have to slow down:

"Emile. It's Ford Madox Ford, 1915. The whole book opens with that line, 'This is the saddest story I have ever heard,' John Dowell says it in the first sentence, and he says heard. You're right that it's strange. But I don't think it's the whole trick. I think it's the door. When I read it I trusted him, because saddest is such a plain word, and then I kept reading and realized he'd already handed me the key to not trusting him, in sentence one, and I took it anyway. The problem isn't whether he lies. It's that he doesn't know he's telling it wrong. Write about the reader, not him. Also Ms. Ong said to look at what he leaves out, not what he says."

He read the photograph twice. It was like Abby to answer a question with a bigger question, and like her to be right anyway. He texted Rogan next, hoping for a blunt second opinion, and got one: "dude it's a book, the guy's a sap, write that he's a sap, 1500 words, go to bed." This did not help, but it made him laugh, and laughing loosened something. He got up, moved the lamp, and started over with two columns on a fresh page: what Dowell says, and where the story disagrees with him.

The column on the right filled faster. Dowell called himself a friend to Edward Ashburnham and a husband to Florence, and every event he narrated quietly dismantled both claims, so that by the middle of the book the words "friend" and "husband" seemed to mean almost nothing. Emile could see the shape of the essay now. The point of view was the engine. Ford had put the reader inside a mind that could not interpret its own evidence, and the reader's job was to become the interpreter Dowell refused to be, which meant the reader's trust was being trained, deliberately, the way a muscle is trained by being torn a little.

The next morning Emile stayed after class to ask Ms. Ong one question. He stood by her desk with the index card in his hand, its edges soft from handling. "If Dowell says he heard it," he said, "can we even call him a narrator? He's acting like a witness to somebody else's tragedy."

Ms. Ong looked at the card, not at him. "What do you call him?"

"I don't know. I think that's the point, actually. I think Ford wanted him unfixed. He tells it like it's a story someone told him over a fireplace, all those old-fashioned storytelling rhythms, and he's inside it." Emile heard himself and worried he sounded like he'd swallowed a study guide. "Maybe the saddest part is that he has to make it a story to survive it. Like an ascetic, almost. He gives up his own claim on his life so it won't hurt him, and it doesn't work."

"That," Ms. Ong said, "is a thesis."

He wrote the essay that night back in the nook, knees folded, the window black behind him. He kept Abby's message propped against the lamp. At the end he typed a paragraph about what he could not settle: whether Dowell was a liar at all, since a liar needs to know the truth, or whether the word "unreliable" was itself too tidy for a man whose whole grammar pushed his own grief into the past tense. He let the paragraph stand. Then he reread the first sentence of the novel one last time, and said it out loud to the empty room, the way you test a stone with a hammer: "This is the saddest story I have ever heard."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In The Broken Column, nails pierce Kahlo's face and body while tears run down her cheeks, yet she looks straight at the viewer.
story:
The community art studio smelled of turpentine and old coffee, and Rachel had claimed the corner table by the window because its light made the print of The Broken Column legible without the overhead glare. Mr. Hu had pinned the reproduction to the corkboard that morning and told the six of them, without ceremony, that by Friday each would deliver a formal critique: colour, composition, symbolism, no biography, no feelings disguised as analysis. Rachel had written the three words at the top of her notebook and then, underneath, nothing.

Ishaan dropped into the chair across from her and slid his own print over, already annotated in green ink. He wanted the studio's summer fellowship, one of two spots, and he had decided weeks ago that formal analysis was his weakness and would be corrected by force. "I've got the palette," he said, tapping the greys and ochres of the ravine that opens in the painted torso. "Muted, anatomical, almost surgical. The column is Ionic, which classically signifies support, and it's shattered, so the symbol works against itself. That's a whole paragraph right there."

"That's true," Rachel said, but her eyes kept going back to the face. The nails. She counted them without meaning to, the small dark heads studding the cheeks and throat and chest, the arms pinned through with them like a map of an injury. And below all of it the tears, bright and deliberate, running in clean tracks. Then the eyes. The eyes were the problem, though she hadn't yet found a way to say what kind of problem.

Hayley leaned over from the next table, chin in her hand. "Honestly, I can't look at it for long. Not because of the nails. Because she's looking back." She laughed a little, embarrassed. "It's like being caught staring at someone's suffering and having them catch you."

Rachel wrote that down, exactly as Hayley had said it, and Ishaan frowned at her notebook. "That's not formal analysis. That's just, like, your personal reaction."

"It's evidence, though," Rachel said slowly. "The gaze is a compositional choice. Every other element pushes inward: the nails, the split torso, the tears running down. The tears run down her cheeks, the nails pierce in, everything about the body says look at me only as a site of damage. And then the eyes do the opposite. They go out. Straight out at the viewer." She turned the print so Hayley could see it again, and Hayley looked for one second and then away, which seemed to Rachel like its own kind of data.

She had spent the previous spring avoiding a similar problem in her own painting, a self-portrait for the school show that she had finally cropped at the forehead because the eyes had refused to come out right and she hadn't wanted to face why. It had been easier to expropriate the style of a painter she admired, all cool blues and distant skies, than to work out what her own face was willing to say. She wondered now whether that had been modesty or cowardice, and whether the difference between the two was anything more than the story you told afterward. She looked at the Kahlo again, at a body made friable, broken open like dry clay, and at eyes that refused the damage any kind of last word.

"Okay," Ishaan said, pulling his print back. "So I write about the contradiction between the inward symbolism and the outward address. Gaze as composition. That actually strengthens my fellowship statement." He was already writing, his pen moving fast, and Rachel watched him take what she had worked out and set it into his own argument the way you'd set a stone into a wall.

"It's yours if you can build it," she said. "I still don't know what to do with the discomfort. Whether it belongs in the critique or just in me." She remembered Mr. Hu saying something once about liminality, about how the best paintings put you on a threshold and then decline to tell you which room you're entering. Maybe that was the honest position: to say that the painting makes a viewer meet its eyes and to admit that she could describe why that was unbearable without being able to resolve it.

On Friday she stood by the corkboard with her notebook open and began, "In The Broken Column, nails pierce Kahlo's face and body while tears run down her cheeks, yet she looks straight at the viewer." She paused, then went on, "Every element pulls downward and inward, and one element does not, and I want to argue that the painting's whole structure depends on that refusal. I also want to admit I can't fully account for it." Mr. Hu nodded once. Somewhere behind her, Hayley whispered, "I still can't look."

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Hans Krebs and William Johnson described the citric acid cycle in 1937, and Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it.
story:
Vanessa had signed the sheet at the front desk like an affidavit: I will complete the Cellular Energy Trail, all eight stations, and my biology teacher would receive the results. Her mother had suggested it after the unit test came back with a red circle around the entire last page, and there had been no arguing, because the alternative was Saturday tutoring with Mr. Patel, who smelled of cough drops and hope.

The science museum's basement was given over to a walk-through cell. Vanessa stood at Station One with her worksheet, a diagram of a glucose molecule sitting there like a six-carbon piece of candy nobody was allowed to eat. Glycolysis, the panel said, splits it in the cytoplasm. She copied the arrow down. Somewhere beyond the foam pillars shaped like organelles, Angelica was texting.

"You skipped the arboreal exhibit," Angelica said when she caught up, nodding at the banner overhead that read Life in the Trees, with its photo of orangutans folded into the canopy. "For this. For a basement."

"Station Three has a wheel you can spin," Vanessa said.

The wheel was the citric acid cycle, painted like a carousel with carbon atoms for horses. Vanessa turned it and watched acetyl CoA climb aboard, watched carbons get clipped off as carbon dioxide, watched a little bulb light up each time the panel said electron carrier. She turned it again. The mitochondrion around her had soft green walls and a low ceiling, and somewhere in the middle of the carousel a brass plaque was screwed into the platform. She leaned over the rail to read it.

Hans Krebs and William Johnson described the citric acid cycle in 1937, the plaque said. Krebs shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it.

"Why does it have a guy's name?" Angelica asked, arriving with a bag of vending machine pretzels. "The cycle. Why is it Krebs's?"

Vanessa read the plaque again, chewing the inside of her cheek. "Him and somebody named Johnson figured it out in 1937. Krebs got the Nobel for it in 1953. Shared it, the plaque says." She straightened up. "So the cycle's named after him and not Johnson. That's the whole answer on this wall, anyway."

"That's it? Johnson does the work and gets skipped?"

"The plaque skipped him." Vanessa spun the wheel again, watched the little bulbs fire. "Maybe there were reasons. Maybe there weren't. It doesn't say." Angelica made a sound through her pretzels that suggested the universe contained a certain amount of this sort of thing and always had.

Station Six was the electron transport chain, a ramp of stepping stones along the mitochondrion's inner wall, and the rule was that you had to walk it while reading each stone's panel aloud. Vanessa did this, feeling ridiculous, feeling sixteen and too old for stepping stones, and yet somewhere around the fourth stone the diagram on her worksheet stopped being a diagram. The carbons she'd watched clipped off at the carousel, the carriers lit up one by one, the stones she was walking: it was all the same glucose, taken apart in stages, and the last stone said ATP, and the wall beside it said the cell spent that ATP on everything, on thinking, on blinking, on the walkthrough she was doing right now.

She stood on the last stone a while. Somewhere behind her, Angelica beseeched her from the exit, saying the orangutans were only upstairs for another hour, saying the pretzels were running low, saying please, Vanessa, the cell is not going to miss you. Vanessa wrote on her worksheet, in the margin where no one had asked for it: the cycle has a name because a person found it, and the prize went around, and the glucose still comes apart either way.

She climbed off the stone and went to hand in her clipboard at the desk. The volunteer stamped it without looking up, which Vanessa found appropriate, given everything. Then she took the stairs two at a time, and found Angelica at the arboreal exhibit arguing with a child about whether sloths were lazy or just efficient.

"Very efficient," Vanessa said. "Like a mitochondrion."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: ISO 216 paper sizes such as A4 have sides in the ratio of 1 to the square root of 2, so cutting a sheet in half gives two sheets of the same shape.
story:
The printer at the back of the public library had two trays, and Alexandra had been staring at them for ten minutes when Jaylynn found her. One tray held A3 paper, the other A4, and the poster file glowing on the screen showed a design she had spent three weekends on: a hand-lettered announcement for the climate walkout, black ink over a wash of storm grey, meant to hang in shop windows all along Jefferson Street.

"Mr. Rodríguez says we get twenty free prints if we're doing school stuff," Jaylynn said, sliding into the chair beside her. She wanted the posters up by Friday, and she wanted them big. "A3. Nobody notices A4."

"I only sized it for A4," Alexandra said. "The margins will go wrong if I stretch it."

Jaylynn leaned over the keyboard, ebullient in the way she got when a plan was already moving in her head and other people had not caught up. "Then stretch it. Nobody measures margins on a poster."

The print dialogue waited on the screen. Alexandra's cursor hovered. She could guess what would happen if she scaled the design up and hope for the best, but guessing felt like the opposite of everything the poster was about, which was evidence, which was the point of a walkout that half the school insisted was just an excuse to skip class. She did not want to prognosticate. She wanted to know.

"Print one of each," she said finally. "Small one first."

Aicha appeared from the stacks with an armful of books on graphic design, checked out for a portfolio she was building whether or not the art teacher approved it. She wanted the walkout posters to credit the design collective the three of them had invented in ninth grade, back when it was only a name on a notebook. She watched the A4 sheet slide out, then the A3, and laid them side by side on the table by the window, where the afternoon light came through in a long pale bar.

Alexandra picked up the A3 sheet, then the A4. She held the smaller one up against the top half of the larger one. Then, with more care, she folded the A3 exactly in half, creased it with her thumbnail, and tore along the fold. The two halves lay on the table. She set the A4 over one of them.

It matched. Edge to edge, corner to corner, the way a key matches a lock.

"The A3 cut in half makes two sheets the same shape as the A4," she said. "Same proportions, exactly. It's the ratio. The sides of A4 are one to the square root of two, so when you cut a sheet in half you get two smaller sheets with that same ratio." She turned the torn half over, checking again. "That's why it scales. That's the whole reason the sizes are built like that."

Aicha frowned at the torn sheet, which was now, technically, ruined for hanging in a window. "You murdered a poster."

"It died for knowledge," Jaylynn said, but she was already re-printing the A3, because the knowledge was worth something: the design could move between sizes without distortion, which meant they could print big for shop windows and small for stapling to telephone poles, and the letters would keep the same shape, the same weight, the same grey. Alexandra set the new sheet on top of the A4 and saw the whole system at once, sizes nested inside sizes, a design that could travel.

Then the wanting began to pull against itself, the way it did. Aicha wanted the collective's name in the corner, small and dignified. Jaylynn wanted the date bigger, wanted the words NO CLASSES NO BUSINESS AS USUAL to hit first. Alexandra wanted the storm grey, which would print muddy on the library's toner and which she had not tested at scale. Each of them had a poster in her head, and the printer could only produce one.

"The grey," Jaylynn said. "Test it or drop it."

"Give me one print."

"You've used nine of the twenty."

"Then I get one more." Alexandra said it without raising her voice, and she was surprised, afterwards, that it had come out steady, because inside she was not steady at all. She had read somewhere that a person's real opinions showed up under constraint, and she was not sure yet whether her opinion was the grey or the compromise or the deadline. She only knew that choosing felt like volition only when she chose it before the deadline chose for her, and Friday was three days away.

Mr. Rodríguez came by with the shelving cart, paused over the torn half-sheet on the table, and said nothing about the waste of paper. He tapped the edge of the A4 where it still lay matched against the torn piece. "You found it," he said. "Most people never ask why the paper is that shape." He rolled the cart on toward the returns bin.

They stayed until the light turned from pale to gold across the table. Jaylynn got her big letters; Aicha got the collective name, set in the corner at exactly the size that felt like credit rather than a signature; and Alexandra got her grey, tested on the tenth print, deep and deliberate, a sky before weather. She kept the torn half-sheet in her binder, between two pages, the fold still visible. At the last minute Jaylynn took the A4 test print, folded it in half, tore it, and set one of the small pieces beside the A3.

"That one's yours," she said. "For the binder."

Alexandra took it.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: The 'guidance hypothesis' from motor learning research holds that feedback after every single attempt can make learners dependent on it, so less frequent feedback often helps retention.
story:
Mr. Wanjiru handed Jack the clipboard on Tuesday and said the seventh-graders were his until the season ended, which was how Jack learned that coaching was mostly a clipboard and the fear of looking down at it. The younger team had one glaring flaw: they could not pass. In drills the ball moved in tidy triangles, and in scrimmages it died at feet, rolled out of bounds, or flew into the fence behind a boy who had turned the wrong way out of pure despair. Jack spent two evenings drawing drills on graph paper, cones arranged like constellations, until his mother asked if it was homework and he said sort of, which felt closer to the truth than he liked.

The first practice, he corrected everything. Every pass earned a verdict. Inside foot, eyes up, plant earlier, softer touch. He was thorough the way only a person who has recently been coached himself can be thorough, repeating phrases he had absorbed without ever examining them. The kids listened. They nodded. They adjusted, pass by pass, and by the end of the hour the triangles looked almost clean.

Saturday they played a game against another school and came apart like wet bread. Jack stood on the sideline shouting the same phrases and the phrases did nothing, because the kids had turned to him after every pass the way sunflowers turn, checking his face for the verdict before deciding what to do next, and a game moves faster than a boy can check. They lost 6-0. In the second half a kid named Tomas stopped looking at Jack entirely, which was somehow worse.

He found Mckenzie in the library on Sunday, because Mckenzie was the sort of person who read about things for fun and had once explained the offside rule to Jack using salt shakers. "There's a thing coaches talk about," she said, scrolling. "The guidance hypothesis. Basically, if you give feedback after every single attempt, learners get dependent on it. They fall apart when you're not there saying things. Less frequent feedback actually helps retention." She turned the laptop so he could see the phrase in a paper dense enough to coagulate the screen. Jack read it twice. "So I taught them to need me," he said. "You taught them to need you," she agreed, and went back to her sandwich.

He did not entirely believe it. Half of him argued that a kid who hears "inside foot" forty times a practice will eventually own "inside foot," the way water wears stone; the other half had watched Tomas's face on Saturday and knew that wearing down was not the same as learning. He sat with the two positions through a study hall, and neither one fully won. What he decided, provisionally, in pencil, was that he had been giving the kids answers when what they needed was the itch of not knowing whether they'd been right.

Monday's practice, he said almost nothing. The cones went down in the same constellation, but now the drill scored itself: gates, a point for a pass through a gate, nothing from Jack. When a pass went wrong he let the silence sit there, friable and uncomfortable, and the kids started talking to each other instead. "You were open late," Braden, the smallest one, told a taller boy, and the taller boy absorbed this with visible suspicion before trying it. Jack bit the inside of his cheek and kept quiet, and felt the quiet cost him something, because being useful was half the reason he'd wanted the clipboard.

By Thursday he had a system he could defend to himself even if he couldn't fully defend it to anyone else. Feedback, but not every attempt. Not even most attempts. He watched for the passes that repeated a mistake three times before he said anything, and when he did speak, he asked questions. "What happened there?" A kid would say "I leaned back," and Jack would nod, and that was all, and the kid would spend the next ten passes leaning forward with the concentration of someone doing long division.

The next game was a 2-2 draw, which in seventh-grade terms was a triumph, though Jack was honest enough with himself to know that one draw proved nothing statistically and something important anyway. The kids did not look at him after every pass. Some of them looked at him not at all, and the ball moved, mostly, in the direction of other kids. He was not sure the guidance hypothesis was the whole story, and he told Mckenzie so at lunch. She shrugged. "That's how hypotheses work," she said. "You keep them in pencil."

He thought about the tryout culture that had made him, the meritocracy of it, every drill ranked, every touch graded, and how good he had been at being graded and how little that had turned out to prepare him for a game where nobody graded anything until afterward. Maybe the truth was somewhere between his two selves, the one who coached with his mouth and the one who coached with gates. He wrote a note on the clipboard for the next practice and underlined it twice, then crossed out one of the underlines.

At the final practice of the season, the kids ran the passing drill without him saying a word. Tomas threaded one through the narrow gate from twenty yards, dead flat, and the whole line made a sound like a kettle starting. Braden turned toward the sideline, caught Jack's eye, and held up one finger, asking without asking.

Jack held up one finger back.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Deliberate practice means working on specific weaknesses with a clear goal and immediate feedback, which improves skill more than simply playing through pieces already known.
story:
The upright bass leaned against the wall of the music classroom like a piece of furniture nobody had ever sat on, and Levi had chosen it for exactly that reason. Nobody else wanted it, so nobody could hear him being bad at it. He had been bad at it since September, and now it was February, and he was still bad in the same specific places: the shift from third position to fifth, and the interval his fingers refused to stretch on the E string.

Across the room, Kaelyn played the opening of her song for what Levi counted as the eleventh time. It was a piano piece from a film about a hotel by the sea, and the first page was lovely and the second page had two bars in it that she had never once played correctly. She always arrived at those bars, slowed down, and turned back to the beginning as if she were greeting an old friend at the door instead of a burglar.

"Play the two bars," said Mr. Addo from the doorway, where he had been watching with his arms crossed. "Only the two bars."

"I'm warming up," Kaelyn said.

"You've warmed up the first page into a puddle. Play bars forty-one and forty-two, ten times, and I'll listen to the whole thing Friday."

She glared at him with the pure, theatrical hatred of someone who knows she has lost. Then she played the two bars. They collapsed. She played them again. They collapsed differently. On the seventh try one of them held together, and Kaelyn stared at her own hand as though it had confessed to something.

Levi watched all this while pretending to tune. He had been doing the opposite of Kaelyn, in a way. He never played anything he knew, because he knew nothing. He played scales, all night if his mother let him, and the scales were smooth and useless, like a road with no destination on it. His fingers were fast now. His fingers were fast and could not play a single piece.

"Mr. Addo," he called, when the teacher drifted past. "Is there a word for what you did to her?"

"Deliberate practice," Mr. Addo said, and kept walking, because he was the kind of man who believed a term was a gift you should not wrap.

Levi sat with it for a moment. Deliberate practice. He thought of Kaelyn's ten repetitions of the ugly bars, each one aimed, each one heard and judged, her face changing as the feedback arrived. Then he thought of his beautiful empty scales. His smoothness was a kind of parasitism, he decided; the pleasure of sounding good was feeding on the time he should have spent sounding terrible. The idea delighted him so much he almost told Kaelyn, then didn't, being circumspect for once, because she was still scowling at bars forty-one and forty-two.

He turned to the piece Mr. Addo had assigned him, found the shift that always failed, and made a mark in pencil: an arrow and the words "here, only here." He played the four notes before the shift and the four notes after it, no more, no less. It sounded like a door being dropped down stairs. He played it again and listened, actually listened, for where the failure began, and it began earlier than he had thought, in his elbow, which he had been imagining was innocent. Jolie, who was shredding quietly on an electric guitar in the corner with her earphones half off, looked up at the noise.

"Was that on purpose?" she said.

"It was on purpose and it was awful," Levi said. "Those are different things."

"Then do it again," she said, and turned her amp down, which he understood, in the strange currency of that room, as an act of generosity. She wanted to hear it, the way you want to watch someone try to open a jar.

He did it again. The fourth time, his elbow did something new. The seventh time, the shift landed late but landed. He had no opinion yet about whether this was improvement or luck, and he held both possibilities open the way you hold two grocery bags. Across the room, Kaelyn played bars forty-one and forty-two one more time, clean, both of them, and then laughed at herself, one sharp note of laughter that cut through the room.

"Again," she said to no one, to everyone.

Levi put his pencil on the next bad bar and drew another arrow.

"Here," he said. "Only here."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The InVID-WeVerify browser plugin, built by a European Union-funded project, splits a video into key frames that can be reverse-searched.
story:
The video arrived in the group chat on Tuesday night, between a photo of Laura's new cat and a debate about whether the physics test had been fair. It showed a street turned into a river, a man clinging to a stop sign while water rolled past his knees, and a caption claiming it was happening right now, two towns over. Jude had shared it with a single word: "insane." Nine people had already forwarded it on.

Alexandra was in the living room with her father's laptop, ostensibly doing homework, when she watched it for the third time. Something about the light bothered her. The caption said now, but the shadows fell the way they did in late afternoon, and the trees along the sidewalk were a green so deep it looked like July rather than October. She had no argument, only a feeling, and she knew a feeling was not a reason to call something false. It was also not a reason to press share.

She remembered the office. In September she'd waited out a school closure at her father's workplace, bored, and a colleague of his, noticing her scrolling, had spun his monitor toward her. He'd shown her a plugin he used before posting anything. "InVID-WeVerify," he'd said, tapping the icon. "Built by a European Union-funded project." It split a video into key frames, he said, frames that could be reverse-searched. He'd dragged one frame into a search bar and, within seconds, found the same image on a news site from three years earlier. Her father had called it the most cautious thing on the internet. The colleague had just smiled and said he preferred to be boring and right.

She found the plugin on her father's laptop, where he'd installed it after that day, and fed it Jude's video. It went to work, the progress bar inching along, and then laid the key frames out in a neat strip like film negatives on a lightbox. The fourth frame, the one with the stop sign and the man's face turned toward the camera, looked promising. She dragged it into the image search and waited, her knee bouncing against the coffee table.

The results loaded slowly, which felt like a small cruelty. When they came, they were not what she expected. The oldest match was not three years old. It was from eleven months ago, a flood in a city four countries away, reported by a regional outlet whose name she could not pronounce. The caption in Jude's video had claimed a place and a present tense, and both were wrong. But the flood itself had been real. People had actually clung to things. The video lied about where and when without lying about what water does.

Laura called while the tabs were still open. "Are you seeing this? My mum's already moved the emergency kit to the front hall." Alexandra explained, haltingly, the frames, the search, the city four countries away, the eleven months. There was a pause with a lot of background in it, someone's television, a door. "So it's fake," Laura said. "It's not exactly fake," Alexandra said, and heard how dour she sounded, like a person determined to drain a room of its emergencies. The flood had happened; the danger being implied here had not. Both of those things were true, and she could not make them into one clean sentence that would stop Laura's mother from moving the emergency kit.

She typed a message to the chat, deleted it, typed another. She wanted something that would correct Jude without lecturing him, but every phrasing she tried had the smell of rectitude, that pleasure people took in being right that made everyone else stop listening. She settled on pasting the link to the original report, adding only, "the same video, last year, different country." Then she sat with her hand above the enter key, aware that she was about to be the person who ruins the video, which was a role with no fans.

Jude's reply came before she'd closed the laptop. "wait, seriously?" Then, a minute later, "how did you even find that." She started to type an explanation, something brief about frames and searches, and stopped, because she could see him rolling his eyes at the length of it. Outside, a neighbour dragged trash cans to the curb, unconcerned about floods. She looked at the blank reply box, and at the strip of key frames still open behind it, and began, slowly, to type.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: John Lewis Gaddis's 1972 book The United States and the Origins of the Cold War, 1941-1947 argued that neither side could bear sole responsibility, a view called post-revisionism.
story:
The air conditioning at her grandfather's house had died again, which was why Kaitlyn was in the study, the one cool room because the trees shaded its windows, sitting on the floor with her back against a shelf of books that smelled like a library from a film about the 1950s. On her phone, Sam had sent forty-one messages since morning, most of them variations of "you have the easy side" and "just say the Soviets started it, done," which was Sam's understanding of the Cold War debate assigned for Monday: Kaitlyn defending the traditional view that the United States bore little blame, Francis arguing the revisionist line that American economic expansion had provoked it.

Kaitlyn had the traditional side, and the problem, as she saw it, was that the traditional side was losing. Francis had already posted sources in the class group chat, whole paragraphs about Open Door policy and atomic diplomacy, and Francis wrote like someone who had done the reading twice. What Kaitlyn had so far was a feeling that things were complicated, which was not, historically speaking, an argument.

She had come to her grandfather's house for dinner and stayed for the study, on the theory that a man who kept sixty years of books could not have nothing on the Cold War. She found the shelf by accident, third from the bottom, where the spines had gone the color of weak tea. The book she pulled out first had a title long enough to require two lines: The United States and the Origins of the Cold War, 1941-1947. John Lewis Gaddis, published 1972. She recognized the date the way you recognize a stranger's face in a photograph from before you were born.

She opened it on the carpet and started reading, and the reading was slow because Gaddis wrote like a man who had been in the archives and wanted you to know it. But a page into the argument she stopped, put her finger under a sentence, and read it again. The book was not taking her side. It was not taking Francis's side either. Gaddis was arguing that neither side could bear sole responsibility, that the thing had been built jointly, out of fear on both ends, and that the honest answer split the blame in ways no debate team would thank him for.

"Grandpa," she called toward the kitchen, "who's John Lewis Gaddis?"

Her grandfather appeared in the doorway drying a bowl, which he did even when the dish rack was full, a habit of holding things. "Professor. Wrote that in seventy-two, the year your mother decided college was for cowards." He set the bowl down. "I read it the summer your grandmother and I were arguing about everything."

"And what did you call someone who says both sides are responsible?"

"Post-revisionist," he said, and picked the bowl back up.

Kaitlyn sat with the word. It was a strange word, the kind that defined itself by what it was not, not the old view, not the revisionist view, a third thing assembled out of refusing the first two. She typed it into her phone and the phone offered her a definition and then, unhelpfully, a shoe brand. In the group chat Francis was still posting, and one of his paragraphs claimed that American planners had wanted economic access to Europe and had therefore engineered the crisis, a tidy little epigram of a claim, and she could see now that it was specious: it sounded complete, and completeness was exactly what was wrong with it. The evidence in Gaddis did not line up behind anyone's tidy claim. The evidence kept behaving like evidence, scattered and contradictory and rude about other people's arguments.

She began drafting on the back of a grocery receipt because her notebook was downstairs. Some sentences she crossed out. "Both sides were responsible" she kept, then worried it was too bare, then worried that worrying about bareness was how people ended up with Francis's paragraphs. What she wanted was the harder thing: to say the traditional view explained some of the record, the revisionist view explained other parts, and Gaddis, this professor from 1972, had weighed the two explanations against the evidence and found neither of them sufficient alone. She could even concede points to Francis, which in a debate was either generosity or a trap, depending on how it was done.

Her grandfather had gone back to the kitchen and returned with two glasses of iced tea, one of which he set on the floor beside her without comment, on a coaster produced from his shirt pocket. He read over her shoulder for a minute. "You know," he said, "your grandmother took the revisionist position. That summer. About the war, about the marriage."

"You had a debate about the marriage?"

"We had several. Gaddis helped me lose gracefully." He tapped the book with his slippered foot. "She kept saying it was all my fault, and I kept saying it was all hers, and then I read this and understood the question was wrong." He said it lightly, the way he said most things, and went to answer the kettle, which had begun to whistle.

Kaitlyn looked at the passage again, at the dates running 1941 to 1947, at the argument that neither side could bear sole responsibility. She texted Sam: "forget what I said about the easy side. I'm conceding half the blame Monday." The reply came back as three question marks, and then, before she could answer, a fourth. She turned the receipt over and kept writing, the ice shifting in her glass beside her, until her grandfather's voice floated out from the kitchen asking whether she wanted the tea sweetened or, as he called it, honest.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: A getter that returns a reference to a private mutable object, such as a list, lets outside code change it, so programmers often return a copy instead.
story:
The pit tables at the regional robotics competition had the atmosphere of a church basement the morning after a flood: cables coiled like sedimentary layers across every surface, zip ties in drifts, and somewhere behind them, a team from Cedar Falls quietly panicking. Xavier spread his laptop open between the battery chargers and pulled up the code for their robot's arm control. Three matches from now, and the arm was still deciding on its own when to close.

The problem lived in his Score class, a tidy little thing he'd written at two in the morning. Private fields, all of them, the way Mr. Bakker had drilled into them until it felt less like a rule and more like a superstition. Integer points, and a private list of scoring events, and getter methods standing guard at the door. He'd been proud of that class. He'd practically laminated it in his mind.

Dane leaned over from the next stool, holding a half-disassembled claw. "Your auton dumped every cube out of bounds, by the way. Denver thinks it's the sensor. I think it's you."

"It's not me. It runs clean on the bench every time." Xavier scrolled anyway, because Dane's suspicion had a way of transmuting into his own, and together they found it faster. The auton code called getEvents, his beautiful getter, and then, in a loop written by their driver module three files away, it cleared the list it got back. Every match, the history went blank, and the arm logic, which counted on that history, did something new and inventive and terrible.

"That's not possible," Xavier said. "The list is private."

"Your list is private," Dane said, with the relish of a boy delivering a verdict. "The thing you handed me is the list."

Xavier stared at the two lines of code as though they'd colluded. He had imagined privacy as a wall, and it turned out he'd built a wall with a window in it, and through the window he was passing the very thing the wall was supposed to protect. He thought of Mr. Bakker saying something once about doors and copies, but the memory was sedimentary, buried under six weeks of sleep debt, and it gave him nothing usable. So he did what he'd learned to do instead of remembering: he wrote a test.

A tiny one. Make a Score, add three events, call the getter, clear what came back, then check the Score's own count. He typed it in the aisle between pit tables while a team from West Des Moines marched past chanting something about their robot's name. He ran it. The count was zero. Three events, gone, and his class hadn't been touched by a single setter. The getter itself had done it, politely, with clean hands.

"Well," said Denver, who had drifted over with a granola bar and no shame about reading other people's screens. "Congratulations. You invented a private field that empties itself. That's not a bug, that's a magic trick."

"It returns the actual list," Xavier said. "Not a copy of it. The actual one." Saying it out loud helped; it stopped being a betrayal and became a fact, the way gravity was a fact, unpleasant mostly when you ignored it. He sat with it for a second, caught between two instincts he could feel arguing in him. Part of him wanted to blame the driver module, because that code was Dane's, and Dane had an egoist's confidence in his own loops. But the louder part, the part that had laminated the Score class, knew the wall with the window was his work. Both things could be true at once, he decided, which was annoying, and he wrote the fix anyway: the getter would hand back a copy from now on, a fresh list, so outside code could empty its own plate and leave his alone.

He reran the test, watched three events survive, and started a fresh build to push to the robot. Dane clapped him on the shoulder and said the arm would still find a way to humiliate them, which felt like gratitude in their currency. The queuing volunteer called their match number. Denver shoved the last cube into the crate, and Xavier closed the laptop, carried it at arm's length through the crowd like something that had finally agreed to behave, and said, "If it drops one cube, you're writing the loops next time."

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Electricity is billed by the kilowatt-hour, so using 600 kilowatt-hours at 15 cents each costs 90 dollars, before any fixed monthly charges.
story:
The laundromat on Fenwick Street smelled like warm lint and detergent, and Jordyn spread her papers across the folding table beside the big dryers, pinning the corners down with a roll of quarters. Two leases, two apartments, both available September first, and she had until Friday to tell her mother which one she meant to sign. The one on Caldwell Street was cheaper by forty dollars a month but the tenant paid all utilities. The one on Hayes Avenue was more expensive and heat was included, but not electricity. She had assumed, until that afternoon, that "utilities" was one blurry number, something you estimated the way you estimated groceries.

Alyvia came in carrying a garbage bag of clothes, which she dropped into a rolling cart with the confidence of someone who had decided to move in with Jordyn before Jordyn had fully decided to move out. "Okay, tell me about the Hayes one," Alyvia said, sitting on the table's edge and swinging her feet. She wanted the Hayes apartment, Jordyn knew, because it was four blocks from campus and because Alyvia believed, without evidence, that Jordyn's mother would co-sign. She had said "we" eleven times in the last two days.

"Rent's six seventy-five," Jordyn said. "Plus electricity, plus internet, plus water, which the landlord says is maybe thirty a month." She turned the lease over. "The Caldwell one is six thirty-five, and the landlord there actually gave me a number. I called him." She had called from the bus, hating the sound of her own voice, and asked the question Ms. Smith had suggested weeks ago when Jordyn stayed after class to argue about budgeting: ask the landlord for the previous tenant's typical usage.

"And?" Alyvia leaned over the pages.

"He said the last tenant used around six hundred kilowatt-hours a month." Jordyn had written it on the back of a receipt. "Electricity is billed by the kilowatt-hour," she said, reading her own note, "so six hundred kilowatt-hours at fifteen cents each is ninety dollars, and that's before any fixed monthly charges, whatever those are." She did the multiplication twice on the paper's margin, because a number that big deserved suspicion. Ninety dollars. Every month. Just for electricity.

"That's it, then, Caldwell wins," Alyvia said immediately, and Jordyn understood that Alyvia had not been listening as a partner but as a lawyer, looking for the clause that got her the Hayes apartment. "Caldwell's cheaper."

"Caldwell's six thirty-five plus ninety plus water plus internet plus heat in the winter, which nobody will tell me," Jordyn said. "And Hayes is six seventy-five plus the same electricity, probably, because the apartments are the same size, plus internet, and heat's in the rent." She lined the two columns up on the receipt. The numbers came out close, closer than the forty-dollar difference had suggested, and the difference that remained depended on heat, which was a winter question and she was doing this in June.

"Don't be revisionist about this," Alyvia said. "Last week you wanted Hayes. You said the light was better."

"That was before the ninety dollars." Jordyn looked at the dryer where her clothes were tumbling, her mother's old work shirts and her own school shirts mixed together, and thought about how the whole apartment decision was really a decision about whether she could afford to emancipate herself from her mother's house without asking for the deposit back in November. Sixty-eight dollars an hour at the garden center. She could do it if the Caldwell number was honest. If the winter heat didn't eat it.

The manager of the laundromat, a woman everyone called Ms. Smith although Jordyn suspected that wasn't the name on the lease of the building, came by with a mop and paused at their table. "Homework?" she said, glancing at the papers.

"Apartment math," Alyvia said.

"Good luck with the fixed charges," Ms. Smith said, and mopped on, which told Jordyn only that fixed charges were real and that Ms. Smith had paid them.

The dryer buzzed. Jordyn gathered the warm shirts into the basket without folding them, the leases sandwiched in the middle of the pile where they wouldn't get wet, and turned to Alyvia, who was still sitting on the table, still swinging her feet, still certain the answer was Hayes. "I'll call the Caldwell landlord again Monday and ask what heat cost last January," Jordyn said. "If he won't tell me, then we sign Hayes, and you walk to campus, and I eat rice until December."

"Rice is fine," Alyvia said. "I'll bring the rice cooker. It's my mom's but she won't notice."

They pushed through the door into the June evening, and Jordyn counted the quarters left in her pocket, three of them, all heads up.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Mexico's Day of the Dead is traditionally celebrated on November 1 and 2, when families build ofrendas, or home altars, with photos and the favorite foods and drinks of relatives who have died.
story:
Austin's mother had cleared the sideboard in the dining room and laid a folded tablecloth over it, and now the whole family stood around the empty surface as though waiting for it to speak. His grandmother had died in March, eight months before this gathering, and the relatives had come from three states to be together over the long weekend. Someone had suggested, at the funeral, that next year they ought to do something proper. Nobody had said what proper meant.

His aunt carried in a cardboard box and set it on the table. "Tia Elena sent these from San Antonio," she said. Inside were sugar skulls still in their cellophane, a bundle of marigolds gone slightly friable at the edges, dried to paper, and a small paper banner cut with skeletons dancing. "She says we're building the ofrenda tonight. Day of the Dead, she says. It's the first and second of November, that's when the families do it."

"Building the what," said Austin's uncle.

"The altar," his aunt said. "The home altar. You put out photos and the favorite foods and drinks of the people who died. Tia Elena was very specific about it."

Austin hung back by the doorway. He had spent the fall applying to colleges, writing an essay about his grandmother without once managing to say anything true about her, and he had a familiar feeling now, the feeling of standing in front of a machine with all the parts spread out and no assembly instructions. In chemistry they had just done polymers, how a single monomer repeated itself into something with actual strength, and he thought about that standing there: how one memory, on its own, was nothing much, and how you could not just name the bond that joined them.

"Her favorite was the pan dulce," his mother said. "From the bakery on Wilson. The pink one, with the sugar on top." She said it to the room but looked at the empty tablecloth. "I don't know if they still make it."

"They do," Austin said. Everyone turned. "I go by there. After my run, sometimes. Saturdays."

"You never told me that," his mother said.

He hadn't told anyone. It had started the week after the funeral, an errand with no reason, and he had kept it because it was his, and because there was something in it he couldn't have explained without sounding like he was performing grief. Now he had said it out loud and the room's attention landed on him like weather.

"Then you'll go," his aunt said, and it was not really a question.

The bakery was three blocks from his grandmother's old apartment, and Mr. Holloway, who had lived across the hall from her for nineteen years, was at the counter when Austin came in. Mr. Holloway had come to the funeral; he had told a story there about his own wife, and a bread she liked, and Austin had half listened. Now the old man recognized him before Austin recognized the recognition, and they stood in line together.

"For the ofrenda," Austin said, when Mr. Holloway asked. "We're building it tonight. Photos and her favorite food. It's a Mexican thing, Day of the Dead, November first and second. I didn't know that until this week."

Mr. Holloway paid for his own bread slowly, counting coins. "My mother's people did something like it," he said. "Different church, same idea. You feed them once a year so you remember to feed yourself the rest of it." He nodded at the pink loaves under glass. "Get two. One for the altar and one to eat. That's the part people get wrong. It's not a museum."

Austin carried the bag home with the warm bread against his palm and turned the words over. Back at the house the ofrenda had begun without him. His cousins had propped the photograph, the one from her seventieth birthday with the cake half cut, and his mother was arranging the marigolds, and Eliot, his cousin's roommate who had tagged along because he had nowhere else to go that weekend, was taping the skeleton banner to the wall with the concentration of a surgeon. Eliot was studying folklore, and Austin had spent an hour that afternoon arguing with him about whether all this was real or whether they were just borrowing a ritual they had no right to. Eliot had said that traditions were borrowed or they died, and Austin had said that was too easy, and he still thought it was too easy, but he watched his mother lift the photograph a quarter inch, adjust it, and leave it, and he thought he understood something anyway. You could hold both. You could do a thing without claiming you owned it.

He set the pan dulce in front of the photograph, then broke off the second loaf and handed pieces around, and people ate it standing up, sugar on their fingers, and his aunt laughed at something and stopped laughing and put her hand on the table edge. His uncle found a bottle of the cream soda his grandmother used to keep for the grandchildren only, and put it on the altar unopened, and nobody said anything about whether it should be opened.

Later, when the aunts and uncles had gone to the kitchen and the cousins were in the yard with Eliot, who was explaining something with his hands, Austin stood alone in front of the little altar. The bread would go stale by tomorrow. The photograph would go back into the drawer, or maybe it wouldn't; nobody had decided. He couldn't tell yet whether the ofrenda had allayed anything or only arranged it, the grief set out in rows like a lab bench, but the room smelled like sugar and marigolds and the cream soda nobody would drink, and he picked up his phone and photographed it exactly as it was.

"Leave the bread," his mother said from the doorway. "Just till morning."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 1950 study by Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter and Kurt Back in student housing found that people living closer together, or near shared stairways, were more likely to become friends.
story:
Dominic counted the boxes from the porch of the house on Alder Row, because counting was something his hands could do while the rest of him refused to be useful. Fourteen boxes, two suitcases, one bicycle with a front wheel he'd have to true before school started. The moving truck had come and gone, and the street was so new to him that the houses looked like they'd been built the night before, which, judging by the pale grass, some of them had.

"You're going to hate it here for about three weeks," his mother said, handing him a broom. "Then you're going to be fine, and you'll feel guilty about being fine."

"That's a speech."

"That's a forecast."

He swept the porch because she asked, and because it gave him a reason to watch the street without looking like he was watching. A girl came around the corner with a dog on a leash, and a man three doors down was setting out a recycling bin in house slippers, and none of them knew him, and that was the whole problem in one sentence.

Sahana lived two houses down, near the shared path that cut between the backyards to the little park at the end of the row. He learned this on the second day, when the dog got loose and Dominic caught its collar at the exact moment it decided the park squirrels were its destiny. "Thanks," Sahana said, slightly out of breath. "He's new here too. We all are, basically. The developer finished this street in spring, so nobody's been here longer than four months." She said it like an apology on behalf of the whole neighborhood, as if newness were a mess she intended to tidy.

By Friday, Dominic had learned that Julius lived in the corner house with the montane view everyone on Alder Row mentioned the way people mention a shared inheritance, and that Julius had already decided the view was better from the second floor, and that he planned to historicize the whole development in a video essay, because a street that went from farmland to forty houses in a year deserved a record of its becoming. "Nobody's going to care," Julius said, not bitterly, just precisely. "Which is why somebody should."
