At school the following week, Dominic ended up beside Sahana in three classes, and beside Julius at a lab table, because alphabet and scheduling had decided these things before anyone's personality got a vote. He found himself telling his old friend Theo on the phone that he missed him and, in the same breath, describing Sahana's impression of their chemistry teacher so precisely that Theo laughed. After he hung up he felt like a traitor to two cities at once, which seemed inefficient, and he lay on his bed turning the feeling over like a wheel that wouldn't true.

The answer arrived, of all places, in a unit on social psychology that Mr. Friedman had them read ahead on. A 1950 study by Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter and Kurt Back, done in student housing, found that people living closer together, or near shared stairways, were more likely to become friends. Dominic read it twice, then looked out his window at the shared path between the backyards. It wasn't that Alder Row contained better people than his old street had. It was that he kept bumping into the same ones, and bumping was apparently where friendship started, in dormitories in 1950 and apparently on new streets now.

He tested it, in his own small way. He started taking the long route to school that passed Julius's corner house, and he lingered on the shared path after walking Sahana's dog when she had early orchestra rehearsal, and within two weeks he knew Julius's sister's name and Sahana's hatred of raisins and the recycling man's passion for the exact model of tractor that had cleared this land. He did not stop calling Theo. But he noticed that the calls got shorter and more honest, because he was no longer calling to hold on to something, only to report from somewhere.

Mr. Friedman caught him after class one afternoon, holding Dominic's worksheet. "You wrote that the housing study was 'reassuring and also a little deflating.' Care to defend that?"

"It means my friends here might just be an accident of geography," Dominic said. "And my old friendships were too, probably. It doesn't mean they're not real. It means I don't get to pretend I chose everything."

Mr. Friedman considered this, then handed back the paper with a small nod that Dominic chose to accept as a grade in itself.

The uncertainty he kept was this: he still didn't know whether he liked Sahana because of the path or because of the way she apologized for the whole street, and he suspected the study couldn't tell him either. On Saturday he trued the bicycle wheel in the driveway, spoking it tight by feel, and Sahana came up the path with the dog and a jar of screws she'd found while unpacking, because she'd noticed his repair stand looked improvised.

"These might be the right size," she said, crouching beside him in the low afternoon light. "Or completely wrong. I didn't check."

"Leave them," Dominic said. "We'll find out together."

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: The electric field between charged plates points from the positive plate toward the negative plate, the direction a positive charge would be pushed.
story:
Grayson had told his mother he didn't need a tutor, didn't need a study group, didn't need anything except the kitchen table and three quiet hours, and this was mostly true, except for the part where Raphael was coming over at seven.

He set his diagram in the middle of the table where Raphael would see it first thing. Two parallel plates, one marked positive, one marked negative, and between them a neat row of arrows he had drawn in green pen. He'd spent forty minutes on those arrows. He'd even made them taper, thinning to points, because the textbook's arrows were ugly and because the whole point of redoing the diagram was that he understood this better than anyone in the class, including Keith, who had gotten a 94 on the last quiz and wouldn't shut up about it.

Raphael let himself in through the back door, the way he always did, and dropped his bag on a chair. "You did the whole worksheet already."

"It's not a worksheet. It's my own diagram." Grayson turned the paper so it faced him. "I'm going to be ready for Tuesday."

Raphael sat down and pulled out his phone, then put the phone face down on the table, which he only did when he was actually going to work. He leaned over the diagram. He was quiet for longer than Grayson liked. "Which one's positive?"

"Top. Obviously, it's labeled."

"So why do your arrows go up toward it?"

Grayson looked at the arrows. They went from the negative plate up to the positive plate, every one of them, beautiful and uniform and wrong in a way he could suddenly see all at once, the way you see the misspelled word on the poster after it's printed. He kept his face still. "It depends how you define it."

"Ms. Adeyemi did this exact thing on the board. She drew it going the other way. I took a picture." Raphael was already scrolling. He turned the phone around. The board photo showed the same two plates, and between them the arrows ran down, from the positive plate toward the negative, fat to thin, the mirror of Grayson's.

Grayson took the phone and held it next to his diagram, side by side, and did not say anything, because the first thing that came into his head was a lie and he knew it was a lie. His mother came through with laundry and said, "Boys, there are cookies," and left again, and neither of them moved.

"Here's what she said," Raphael said. "She said ask where a proton would go. Like, if you stuck a proton in there, which way would it get pushed."

Grayson had written that in his notes. He found the page, two days back, in his own handwriting: positive charge, pushed, plates. The arrows he'd drawn pointed toward the plate that would pull a proton in and hold it, not away from the plate that would shove it. He had drawn the direction a proton would be dragged, not the direction it would be pushed, and he had done it with confidence, in green pen, for forty minutes. The kitchen light buzzed. His mother's footsteps went up the stairs.

"So the field," Raphael said. "It goes from the positive plate to the negative one."

"From the positive plate toward the negative plate," Grayson said. It came out flat. He wasn't correcting Raphael, he was making himself hear it, the way you repeat an address so you don't walk to the wrong house.

"And that's the direction a positive charge would be pushed. A proton. That's the whole test."

Grayson pulled the diagram back and turned his pen over, but he didn't erase. Erasing felt like admitting something, and he wasn't sure yet what he was admitting. He thought about the taxonomies Ms. Adeyemi was always building on the board, pushing everything into its column, conductors and insulators, series and parallel, and how he'd filed tonight under "already mastered" before he'd checked a single fact. He'd been profligate with his certainty, spending it everywhere, on the arrows, on the claim that he didn't need Raphael, on the 94 he was going to get Tuesday. And the worst part wasn't the arrows. The worst part was that the diagram still looked right to some part of his brain, the same part that had told him he was ready.

He erased the arrows. All of them, down to the smudge. Then he drew new ones going the other way, and this time he stopped at the first one and checked it against the board photo, and checked the second one, and by the third he stopped checking, not because he was confident again but because checking each one felt like a habit worth having and also like something he could stop doing when it stopped being useful. Somewhere in there was a line between trusting himself and testing himself, and he could not have said exactly where it fell.

Raphael took a cookie when his mother brought the plate down, and ate it watching Grayson draw. "You know Keith got a 94," he said.

"I know."

"He drew his arrows wrong too. I saw it. He argued with her for like five minutes."

"Did he erase his?"

"Are you kidding? He's still wrong. He's photocopying his notes for the whole group tomorrow."

Grayson finished the last arrow, from the positive plate down toward the negative, the way a positive charge would be pushed, and set the pen on the table. "Don't tell him," he said. "Let him ask me."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Spanish news writers often attribute a claim with 'según', meaning 'according to', which tells a reader the statement comes from a source, not the reporter.
story:
The hostel in Granada had one table by the window, and Connor claimed it before his parents were awake, the newspaper folded to page four like it had been waiting for him all week. He had told Ms. Eze, before the trip, that he didn't need the practice packet. He'd told Holden the same thing, twice, leaning against the locker with his chin up. "I test well," he'd said. "That's not the same as knowing a language," Holden had said, and Connor had laughed, because it was the same thing. It was obviously the same thing.

The assignment was simple on paper: find a short article, read it, summarize it aloud, record the summary, send it to Ms. Eze by Friday. He'd chosen one about flooding in the south, three paragraphs, a photograph of men in waders carrying a sofa through brown water. He read the first sentence four times. Then five. The dictionary app on his phone kept offering him words he already knew and refusing the ones he didn't, as if it had chosen a side.

His mother came down in her tourist clothes and put coffee in front of him without asking whether he wanted it. "How's the homework?" she said. "Done," he said, which was true in the sense that he had started it. He waited until she'd gone up for her sunglasses. He was, he told himself, a strong reader in English, and strength transferred. It transferred in weightlifting. It transferred in math.

The trouble was the second paragraph. It said the dam had been opened without warning, that officials had known for hours, and then it said, "Según el portavoz del ayuntamiento, la alerta se envió a tiempo." He copied the sentence into his notebook and stared at it. Según. He'd seen it before, in a list of prepositions he'd memorized in one sitting and then never used. He typed it into the search bar, and the translation came back: "according to."

So the sentence wasn't saying the alert was sent on time. He wrote that down, then crossed it out, then wrote it again. According to the town hall spokesperson, the alert was sent on time. The words came from the spokesperson. The reporter had put the claim in the paper, but the reporter hadn't made the claim. That was the whole point of the word sitting there at the front of the sentence, doing its quiet work. In English, Connor realized, he read right past "according to" a hundred times a week, skimming toward the juicy part, filing claims as facts because the facts sounded better.

He texted Holden. Is segun like according to. Holden wrote back eight minutes later, long enough that Connor imagined him playing a game, being casual, being free. "yeah, según means according to. Spanish papers use it all the time." Connor stared at the little accent mark. He had been about to say, out loud, into his recording, that the town hall had sent the alert on time, that the whole thing was a misunderstanding, and now he understood that the paper had never said that at all. Someone quoted in the paper had said it. His face went hot in a way that felt visceral, the embarrassment located somewhere behind his sternum like a swallowed coal.

He tried the summary aloud, alone, the phone flat on the table. "El artículo trata de las inundaciones," he began, and his voice came out steadier than he felt, which he decided meant he felt steady. He worked through it. Two dead, twelve evacuated, fields under water. And then the part he'd nearly botched. "Según el portavoz, la alerta se envió a tiempo. Pero los vecinos dicen que no recibieron nada." According to the spokesperson, sent on time. But the residents said they received nothing. The paper printed both. The paper wasn't deciding. He was the one who had almost decided, without noticing, in the two seconds between reading and repeating.

Ms. Eze had said something once about learning to historicize a source, to place it, to ask who was speaking and from where, and at the time it had sounded like something teachers said to fill the period. Now he could feel the shape of it. He still didn't know, and could not know from three paragraphs, whether the spokesperson was lying or the residents were confused or both were partly right. That bothered him more than the vocabulary had. He could memorize words. He could not memorize the truth about a flood in a valley he'd never seen.

He pressed record. He gave the summary once more, slow, careful, the según in its right place like a load-bearing wall. Then he attached the file and set the phone face-down on the newspaper, over the photograph of the sofa in the brown water, and watched two men in waders struggle with it toward dry ground.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In a standard repayment mortgage, early monthly payments go mostly toward interest, and later payments go mostly toward paying down the amount borrowed.
story:
Eric set two envelopes on the kitchen table and did not open either one. The first was addressed to his mother in a windowed envelope, the kind that looked official, the kind that could be a bill or something worse, something like a subpoena, though he knew that was a word for court and this was probably only rent. The second envelope was thinner and had no window, and it had come through the door slot that morning with a soft sound he'd heard from his room. His mother was at work. He sat down across from her cold coffee and put one finger on the thick envelope.

His cousin was already at the table, because she'd come over the night before after her shift and slept on the couch, and she was eating cereal with her phone propped against the sugar jar. "Don't open that," she said, without looking up. "It's never good news before nine in the morning." She was twenty-four, had a house, which to Eric made her a kind of adult success story, and she had been up half the night looking at something on her phone with a face he couldn't read.

"It's rent," Eric said. "It's always rent." Their building had been sold in the spring, and the new management company sent envelopes like this one every few months. His mother had explained the system to him once: you paid rent every month, and when you first moved in you also paid a security deposit, a month's worth of money held by the landlord in case you damaged the place, returned to you when you left if you didn't. He'd asked once why they couldn't just buy a place instead, and his mother had laughed in a way that wasn't really laughter and said that buying needed a down payment first, tens of thousands of dollars saved up before a bank would even talk to you.

"Open it, then," his cousin said, and put down her spoon.

The letter inside said that at the end of their lease term, the rent would go from eleven hundred a month to fourteen fifty. Eric read it twice. Fourteen fifty was most of what his mother brought home in a good month. The feeling arrived in his body before it arrived anywhere else, a somatic thing, his hands cold and his stomach tight, as if his nerves had voted before his mind got a say.

"That's insane," his cousin said, leaning over his shoulder. Then she slid her phone across the table, screen up. "Look at this, anyway. You want to talk about insane." On the screen was a statement from her bank, a mortgage statement, and she tapped a line near the bottom. "Five years I've been paying. Five years, every month, never missed one. Look what I still owe. It barely moved. It's like the money goes into a hole."

Eric looked at the number she'd paid over five years and the number she still owed, and then at the number she'd owed at the start, printed on an earlier page she scrolled to. He did the subtraction on the back of the rent letter, pencil scratching in the margin. She'd paid out a fortune and the amount she owed had gone down by almost nothing. He turned the pages back and forth, and the pattern showed itself: the early statements showed the same debt month after month, and only recently had the number started to slip, slowly, like a tide going out.

"So the first years of payments," he said slowly, "they're mostly going to the interest. Not to the actual house. And later, the payments mostly go to paying down what you borrowed." She stared at the screen as if the words had rearranged it. "So I'm five years in," she said, "and I've basically just been renting money."

The dread Eric had been carrying all morning coagulated into something with a shape. He thought of the new owners of his building, whoever they were, somewhere in an office, and he thought of Mr. Grant, the old man who had owned it before, who used to fix the lobby light himself. And here was the thing he'd been chewing since he read the letter, the thing that made him stand up and walk to the window over the sink: the new company's letterhead matched the name on his cousin's bank statement. The people raising their rent by three hundred and fifty dollars were a mortgage lender, and somewhere in their books his building was a debt being paid down month by month, mostly interest, barely moving, exactly like his cousin's house.

"We could ask them," his cousin said behind him. "At the office. Today."

Eric folded the letter along its crease and put it in his jacket pocket, along with the deposit receipt his mother kept in the drawer by the fridge, the paper that proved they'd paid to live here before any of these people owned it.

"Get your shoes," he said.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Raising the temperature speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions, but it speeds up the endothermic direction more, which is why the equilibrium shifts that way.
story:
The chemistry wing of the science museum smelled like hand sanitizer and old carpet, and Riley had walked past the equilibrium demonstration three times before he stopped at it. He had a quiz to retake on Monday, and the question he'd missed was still sitting in his notebook, circled twice: what happens to a reaction at equilibrium when you raise the temperature? He'd written that everything speeds up, forward and reverse, so nothing changes. His teacher had drawn a single red line through it and written see me, and Riley had not gone to see him. He had come here instead, because Carmen said the museum had tubes you could heat yourself.

Carmen was already at the table, holding one of the sealed glass tubes up to the light. Inside was a gas, pale brown, almost the color of weak tea. "It's nitrogen dioxide," she said, reading the placard. "It's in equilibrium with something. Dinitrogen tetroxide, which is colorless. So the color tells you which way it's shifted. More brown means more of the brown stuff."

"Forward and reverse," Riley said. "Both happening at the same time, same rate. That's what equilibrium means." He knew that part. He had known that part on the quiz too. The part he'd gotten wrong came after.

Rayan showed up with a paper bag of vending machine pretzels and leaned on the table. "Mr. Do said to meet him here at two. He's judging the bridge-building thing downstairs." Mr. Do coached the robotics team all three of them had been on, and he had a habit of appearing wherever students were struggling with something, as if their confusion carried a signal he could pick up.

The table had a basin of hot water and a basin of ice water, both looking less than sanitary. Riley took a tube, rolled the gas around, and lowered it into the hot basin. He kept his thumb on the top of the tube even though it was sealed, which Carmen noticed and did not comment on.

Nothing happened for a second. Then the gas darkened, fast, going from weak tea to strong tea to something like cola. Riley lifted it out, held it against the white placard, and watched the brown hang there. He put it in the ice water and it faded just as quickly, back to almost nothing. He did it again. Heat, dark. Cold, pale. The gas seemed to change color of its own volition, which was the part that had never made sense to him. Nothing was added. Nothing was taken away. Just temperature.

"That's not what I said on the quiz," Riley said. He set the tube down in the rack, where it stood among a dozen others, some of them so old their labels had gone friable and were crumbling off in little flakes whenever someone touched them. "I said heat speeds up both directions, so the rates stay equal and nothing shifts. Both reactions are happening in there, right? Heat should just make them both faster."

"Maybe it speeds them up different amounts," Carmen said. She took her own tube and dunked it. "Like, one of them gets more out of the heat than the other one does."

Riley stood with his hands on the edge of the basin. The water had gone lukewarm against his wrists. "Okay, so both directions speed up," he said slowly. "But the one that's endothermic, the one that takes in heat, that one speeds up more. It gets more out of it because it's the one using the heat." He picked up the tube again. "In this one, the brown stuff must be the endothermic direction. So when I heat it, the brown direction speeds up more than the other direction, and the whole thing shifts toward brown. The color's not just moving faster. It's actually a different mixture now."

Rayan, who had been eating pretzels through all of this, pointed at the tube with a pretzel. "So cold would do the opposite. The other direction is the one that gives off heat, so the mixture goes that way." He reached over and put the tube in the ice basin himself. It faded. "So on your quiz, the answer was that it shifts."

"The answer was that it shifts toward whichever direction is endothermic," Riley said. He said it twice in his head to make sure he had it straight, because he wanted to be able to say it again on Monday without the tube in his hand. "Speeds up both, but that one more. That's the whole thing." He looked at the rack of tubes, at the placard with its equations, at the basins. There was a question still bothering him, and he could not quite close it. "What I don't get is why. Why does the endothermic one get more out of heat? Nothing here tells me that."

Mr. Do arrived before anyone could attempt an answer, carrying a clipboard and a coffee. He looked at the tubes, the basins, the three of them, and raised his eyebrows. "Ah," he said. "The equilibrium demo. Someone finally using this wing for its intended purpose instead of as a shortcut to the restrooms."

"I got the concept," Riley said. "But the why is still open."

"Good," Mr. Do said. "Write that down as a thing you know and a thing you don't. That's a longer list than most people keep." He checked something off on his clipboard and moved on toward the elevators.

Riley took out his phone and typed it under the circled question: speeds up both, endothermic more, shifts that way, why = still open. Then he picked up a fresh tube from the rack, held it to the light, and lowered it into the hot water to watch it turn brown one more time.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: The force on a charge in an electric field equals the charge times the field strength, F = qE, so doubling the charge doubles the force.
story:
The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and hot extension cords, and somewhere behind the folding tables a custodian's radio played a station that had given up on the current decade. Alexandra spread her poster boards across the last available table and weighted the corners with the batteries she was no longer using, since her capacitor project had turned out, in Ms. Van Dijk's word, moribund. The dielectric had cracked overnight. What remained was a single working demo: two aluminum plates on a stand, a ruler taped between them, and a handwritten sign that said ASK ME ABOUT FIELD STRENGTH.

"You can't win with that," Alisa said, arranging her own display, which involved a laptop, a speaker, and a title with a colon in it. "It looks like a bake sale."

"It looks like physics," Alexandra said, though privately she agreed. She had spent three weeks on the capacitor and four hours on this, and the unfairness of that arithmetic sat in her stomach like a swallowed stone.

Ms. Van Dijk came by during setup, holding a clipboard and the permission forms that had made the vice principal talk about liability, about how the school could not indemnify students for homemade equipment, as though Alexandra's plates were somehow going to sue somebody. "Where's your particle?" Ms. Van Dijk asked. She tapped the empty space between the plates. "You computed the field between them. Four hundred volts, two centimeters apart. So you have a number. Now make the number do something."

Alexandra had made the number do nothing all morning. She knew the field strength; she had divided the voltage by the separation and gotten twenty thousand volts per meter, and she could say it forward and backward. But a value with nothing acting inside it was like a verdict with no trial. Behind her, Alisa was rehearsing a speech about sound frequencies to a row of middle schoolers who were mainly interested in whether the speaker could play anything by anyone they had heard of.

Daniyal arrived at lunch with pita bread and an apology about the capacitor, which he had helped solder and which he still referred to as "our baby," despite its having died. He stood in front of her table with his chin in his hand, the way he did when he was deciding whether to argue. "You need a charged dust particle," he said. "Something small. Put it in the field and watch it move."

"Great. Where do I get one?"

He looked at the floor, which was grey with years of wax and dust, and then at her, and grinned. "Everywhere. You're standing in a supply."

They spent the fair's second hour not winning. Daniyal rubbed a grain of foam packing material on his sweater until it clung to his finger, and Alexandra borrowed the multimeter from a boy whose project on soil pH had already been abandoned for a card game. She measured the little charge as best she could, something on the order of a few nanocoulombs, and then stood at the table with her calculator, doing what she should have done at ten that morning. The force on a charge in a field was the charge times the field strength. She typed it, looked at it, typed it again. Her grain carried a tiny charge, and the field she had computed pushed on it with a force she could actually calculate, and when Daniyal asked what happened if the grain held more charge, she punched in double the value and the force came out double too. It was the same field either way. The field did not care. Doubling the charge doubled the force, and that was all there was to it, and she felt the small click of it settling into place, the way a key feels when it finally turns.

"F equals q E," she said out loud, mostly to the poster.

"Say it again with conviction," Daniyal said. "Judges are circulating."

The foam grain, when she released it between the energized plates, drifted sideways and stuck to the positive plate like a confession. A judge with a lanyard watched, asked her what the subpoena of the particle had been, which was either a joke or a genuine confusion about the vocabulary, and Alexandra answered the question she wished had been asked: the force had been the charge times the field, small but real, and the grain had gone exactly where the arithmetic said it would. The judge nodded, wrote something, moved on to Alisa's speaker, where the middle schoolers had assembled again like a jury.

At four o'clock the ribbons went up. Alisa took second in physical science, and her laptop played a tinny fanfare while people clapped, and she hugged Alexandra hard enough to knock a battery off the poster board. Alexandra's name was not called. Her table had drawn eleven visitors, two of them lost, and the moribund capacitor sat boxed under the folding table like a relative nobody wanted to discuss.

But the foam grain was still stuck to the positive plate when she packed up, and she peeled it off and held it on her fingertip in the wax light, this speck that had been pushed by a field she had measured and a force she had predicted, and she put it in the pocket of her jeans instead of the trash.

"You're keeping it," Daniyal said. It wasn't a question.

"I'm keeping it," she said, and folded the table's legs in.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: An 'I-message', popularized by psychologist Thomas Gordon, states the speaker's own concern, such as 'I'm worried we'll miss the deadline', instead of accusing the listener with 'you' language.
story:
The email had been open on Maika's laptop for forty minutes, and it still said only "Hi Juliana." Behind it, through the library window, the fog was burning off the football field, evanescent in the way that October mornings were, present and then simply not. Juliana had left her school store shift early again on Thursday, which meant Maika had counted the register alone, which meant she had missed the bus and walked home in the dark. She wanted to say so. She did not want to say it in a way she would regret.

Her first attempt read: "You keep leaving early and it's not fair." She stared at it, then typed below it: "You clearly don't care about the store at all." That one was worse. It imputed a motive she couldn't actually see; Juliana might care enormously and still walk out at three, for reasons that had nothing to do with the register or the bus or Maika. She deleted both drafts and put her head in her hands.

Mr. Ferreira passed behind her on his way to the copier, and she minimized the window out of instinct, though he supervised the store and had every right to read what she was writing. "Ferreire," as Guneet insisted on misspelling it in every text, had told them only, "You two need to sort it out yourselves." Which was a way of saying nothing, Maika thought, while sounding like a way of saying everything.

Guneet dropped into the chair across from her with a biology textbook cracked against the table. "Speciation quiz Monday," she said. "Ask me what happens when a population gets geographically isolated."

"What happens?"

"It stops sharing genes and eventually it's a different species. Two groups that used to be the same thing can't even talk to each other anymore." Guneet looked up at that, as if she'd heard herself. "That's not about finches, is it."

"Juliana left early again."

"You're going to send her something you can't take back." It wasn't a question. Guneet leaned over and read the empty draft, the cursor blinking after the greeting. "Last year in peer mediation training they made us rewrite everything. There's this thing, it's called an I-message. Some psychologist, Thomas Gordon, came up with it." She turned the laptop toward herself. "Watch. Instead of 'you keep leaving early,' you say what's actually going on for you."

So it wasn't "you abandoned me"; it was "I was worried we'd miss the deadline for the deposit count, and I ended up alone at closing." Maika typed it slowly, testing each phrase. The sentence felt exposed, almost embarrassing, because it admitted to the worry instead of hiding behind the accusation. She wrote that Thursday's closing had taken an hour, that she'd missed the bus, that she wanted to agree on a plan for who stayed until the count was done. She asked, in the last line, whether something was making three o'clock difficult, and said she'd take any shift that worked better for Juliana's schedule. She did not mention fairness. She did not mention not caring. Rereading it, she could see that a structured email, the kind with a subject line and a numbered suggestion, sounded cold to her ear but clear to everyone else's, and she decided clear was what she wanted, and left it.

She hesitated over the send button, because the worry underneath the worry was that this was too polite, that politeness was its own accusation, that Juliana would read the formality and understand it as a verdict. There was no way to control that. Maika sent it anyway, closed the laptop, and pulled Guneet's textbook toward her to be quizzed on isolation and gene flow, which she promptly failed.

Juliana replied during fifth period. "I didn't know you missed the bus. My brother's pickup broke and I've been getting him from middle school. I should have told you. Can we talk at lunch?" Maika read it twice under her desk. It didn't fix anything yet; Thursday was still Thursday, and she still didn't know whether a plan would hold past the first week. But the message was long, and the word "sorry" appeared in it, and at the bottom Juliana had typed, "also your email didn't sound like a lawsuit, it sounded like you."

At lunch Juliana was already at the corner table with two trays, one pushed across for Maika, and a printout of the store's closing checklist between them, pen already in hand. "Okay," she said, tapping the last line, where it said the count must be witnessed by two people. "Tell me exactly what you need from me, and I'll tell you what I can actually do."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Ontario high school students must complete 40 hours of community involvement to earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma.
story:
Ryder had signed up on Tuesday because the deadline on the school portal had turned red, and by Saturday morning he was standing in the basement of a church on Dunham Street, tying a too-large apron behind his back while a woman named only in his head as the coordinator pointed him toward a wall of stainless steel trays. Forty hours. He needed forty hours of community involvement before June or he would not graduate with his Ontario Secondary School Diploma, and he had left it, in the way he left most things, until the last possible Saturday. The fact sat in his phone like a debt. He had six hours banked from a park cleanup in grade ten and nothing since.

His job was the bread table. Zavier from his economics class was already there, stacking buns with the bored competence of someone who had done this many times, and it was Zavier who told him the system: two per guest, ask before you hand over the seeded ones, and never touch the bruised fruit because the guests will take it out of politeness and then not eat it. "You're here for hours, aren't you," Zavier said, not quite a question. "It's fine. Half the grade twelve line is."

Sarah-Maude arrived twenty minutes late with her hair still wet, having biked, and took the ladle at the soup station. She was the sort of person who had finished her forty hours in grade nine and kept coming anyway, which Ryder found either admirable or performative and could not decide which. He was, in general, suspicious of goodness that came easily. His own motivations were legible and small: a diploma, a red number on a screen, a mother who had stopped asking. That honesty was, he thought, at least worth something.

At eleven the doors opened and the room filled with the smell of onions and wet wool. A man with forearms like dock rope took his two buns and then stood there, and Ryder understood he was expected to say something, and could not think what. "Cold out," the man offered, and Ryder said it was, and the man said it would be colder tonight, and moved on. The exchange left Ryder with a thin foreboding, a sense that he was performing a kindness he had not earned, and that everyone in the line could see the seams of it.

The twelfth guest was Mr. González, his old grade ten history teacher, wearing a coat Ryder recognized from class, the gray one with the elk buttons, now shiny at the elbows. Mr. González saw him at the same moment and there was a small rearrangement in his face, the effort of deciding how much to acknowledge. "Ryder," he said finally, warmly enough. "You're volunteering." Not a question. "Hours," Ryder said, and hated how fast he said it, and Mr. González nodded as though this were a reasonable answer, which made it worse. He took his soup to a corner table and ate slowly, reading a paperback, and did not look over again.

Ryder worked through the lunch rush in a state he could only call cerebral, turning the same few thoughts like coins in a pocket. On one side: he was here for himself, for a requirement, and the soup kitchen was functioning as an extension of his transcript. On the other: his hands had ladled and stacked and carried for three hours, and the food had gone into actual people, and none of those people cared what was written on his form. Zavier, when Ryder floated this at the dish pit, shrugged under the steam. "Requirement's why I came. It's not why I come back." Which was either a distinction or a dodge, and Ryder couldn't tell.

He found himself near the corner table during the lull, wiping it down without having been asked. Mr. González closed the paperback on his thumb. "You know I student-taught for free for two years before anyone paid me," he said. "Everyone starts somewhere impure." Ryder said he didn't think it was impure exactly, and Mr. González said that was the right answer to the wrong question, and reopened his book, and that was the entire conversation.

Near two o'clock, Sarah-Maude brought him the sign-out sheet and a pen, and he wrote his name and the hours, four and a half, in the column, and felt the small mechanical pleasure of a number going up, and the small corresponding cost of feeling that pleasure at all. He looked down the sheet at the other grade twelve names stacked above his, everyone chasing the same forty, and thought that the diploma requirement had manufactured this whole afternoon, his labor and Zavier's and the bread on the table, out of a policy line in a curriculum document. He also thought that the man with the dock-rope forearms had eaten, and would not have cared about the mechanism. Both things were true and neither cancelled the other, and he could not resolve them, and suspected the resolution, if there was one, was not his to have at eighteen.

Outside, the cold found the damp patches on his sleeves. Sarah-Maude unlocked her bike and said, "Same time next Saturday? Zavier's on bread again." Ryder stood with his hands in his pockets, his sign-out slip folded in quarters, four and a half hours closer to a number that would let him out of high school and into whatever came next. "I don't know," he said. "Maybe." She swung onto the seat and waited a beat, as if the maybe had weight, and then pushed off down Dunham Street, and he watched her go, and started walking the other way.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: By the second derivative test, if f'(a) = 0 and f''(a) is negative, the function has a local maximum at x = a.
story:
Aidan's grandfather had measured the strip of grass behind the shed three times before breakfast, and now the tape lay coiled on the porch rail like something exhausted. Twenty meters of chicken wire, that was the fixed quantity, and the run would back against the shed wall so only three sides needed fencing. "I want the hens to have the most room we can give them," his grandfather said, wiping his hands on his trousers though they were already clean. "Your grandmother says they malign the whole backyard if they're cramped, and she's usually right."

Aidan had brought his math notebook on the train because summer homework did not cancel itself, and because Ms. Morales, his teacher, had written a single comment in red at the bottom of his last test that he had been carrying around like a stone: "You find the critical points. You stop there. Finish the thought." It was not scathing, exactly. She was not a scathing person. But it was shorter than her usual comments, and the brevity stung more than a paragraph would have.

He sat on the porch steps with the notebook open and drew the run. If the two sides sticking out from the shed were each x meters, then the far side, parallel to the wall, used the rest of the twenty: 20 minus 2x. The area inside was x times (20 minus 2x), and when he multiplied it out he got a polynomial, 20x minus 2x squared. He wrote it at the top of a fresh page and underlined it twice, which was a habit his mother called dramatic and which he defended as organizational.

The difficulty was not drawing the picture or writing the function. The difficulty was that he did not know how to find the x that made the area biggest, and his grandfather was already standing at the rail again, holding a spade, waiting on an answer with the patience of a man who had waited on many things. Aidan texted Pedro, who had taken the same class and scored higher on the same test.

"i know this one," Pedro wrote back within a minute. "derivative. power rule. it's in ch 3." Then, a few seconds later, a second message: "the derivative is where it changes. slope of the curve. don't ask me why it works at 7am." Aidan did not ask why. He applied the power rule to 20x minus 2x squared and got 20 minus 4x, and then he set that equal to zero because that was what you did, apparently, and 20 minus 4x equals zero gave x equals 5. Five meters out from the wall, ten meters across, fifty square meters of run.

But staring at the number 5, he felt the exact hollowness Ms. Morales's comment had been pointing at. How did he know that x equals 5 gave the biggest area and not the smallest? What if the curve dipped there instead of peaking? He imagined the hens standing in the bottom of a valley of bad choices while his grandfather drove posts into the wrong ground. He wrote to Pedro again: "how do i know 5 is a max and not a min." The reply took longer this time, long enough that Aidan could hear his grandmother inside rinsing coffee cups, and when it came it was unhelpfully calm: "you could just check numbers on either side. or man up and do the second derivative test."

The textbook was in the trunk of the car, because his grandfather kept the trunk of the car the way other people kept a library, and Aidan retrieved it with the spade still watching him. The chapter on the second derivative was short and, to his relief, free of bromides about practice making perfect. He read it once, then again, and then a third time at the top of the steps, because what it said was so spare it seemed almost rude: by the second derivative test, if f prime of a equals zero and f double prime of a is negative, the function has a local maximum at x equals a. He said it out loud to the yard. "Local maximum," he said, and the words felt like a tool with a proper handle.

So he differentiated again. The derivative of 20 minus 4x was minus 4, a flat, stubborn number, negative everywhere, negative at 5, negative wherever anyone cared to look. He checked the terms against the page twice, because Pedro's "or man up" had the tone of a dare and dares made him careless. Zero at the top, minus 4 underneath. A peak, not a valley. He sat with that for a moment, honestly unsure whether he understood it or had merely executed it, and decided that the distinction could wait for September, for Ms. Morales, for a classroom where someone would ask the question he did not yet know how to phrase. What he had was enough to dig on, and his grandfather had already chosen a corner for the first post.

They set the posts at five meters out, and while his grandfather tamped the earth, Maggie arrived on her bicycle with a folded note in the basket, because Maggie distrusted phones the way other people distrusted large dogs. He unfolded it on the porch rail. "Morales posted the bonus problem," she had written in her narrow, urgent hand. "Same shape as the garden thing. She says anyone who shows the second derivative gets the extra credit. I got the same thing you got, minus four, so either we're both right or we're wrong in a very organized way. Come by if you want to check it before Monday. P.S. tell your grandfather the hens were maligning the old coop all spring, they'll like this one better."

Aidan read the note twice and laughed at the last line, and then carried it out to where his grandfather was unrolling the chicken wire along the new posts, the silver mesh catching the late light. He held the paper out. "It's maximum," he said. "Fifty square meters. I did it twice to be sure." His grandfather took the note, read it slowly, nodded at the part about the hens, and handed it back, and then he said, "Hand me that wire, then. The birds move in Saturday," and the two of them bent to the work together.

story:
The quiz came back on a Tuesday, folded once, a red 71 at the top like a small wound. Ella had found the critical point perfectly. She had set the derivative to zero, solved, circled her answer, and moved on, certain. Ms. Becker had deducted the last six marks with a single stroke and no comment, which was worse than a comment, because it left Ella to metabolize the failure on her own, without knowing its shape.

"It's the interval," Everleigh said at lunch, leaning over the paper between their trays. "Look. It says on the closed interval from zero to five. You found where the derivative is zero, but you never checked the ends." She tapped the printed numbers. "Charlie got the same thing wrong."

"I checked my arithmetic four times," Ella said. "That wasn't the problem."

"Obviously." Everleigh was never unkind, only brisk, the way she was in field hockey. "The problem is you thought there was only one place to look."

After school Ella found Charlie in the emptying chemistry lab, rinsing beakers he hadn't used, which was his way of putting off going home. He showed her his quiz, the identical red stroke, the identical silence. "I asked Ms. Becker after class," he said. "She just said, 'The endpoints.' That was it. Like I was supposed to feel stupid and grateful at the same time." He laughed, but the laugh had a choleric edge, and he set the beaker down harder than the beaker deserved.

That night Ella sat with her textbook open and her quiz beside it, working the same problem a third time, then a fourth. The polynomial rose, peaked where she had said it peaked, and then, on the far side, it climbed again, higher than the peak, all the way to the right endpoint of the interval. She checked the value there. It was bigger. On a closed interval, the largest value could sit at an endpoint where the derivative was not zero at all, and if you never tested the ends, you would report a maximum that was only local, a summit that was not the summit. She sat with that for a while. It felt less like math and more like something being quietly corrected in her.

She had applied to seven colleges and told no one the order of her preferences, not even Everleigh, because the order kept changing. In her inbox was a message from her older cousin, sent that morning, and she opened it now, needing a reason not to look at the graph again.

Ella, the message read, you asked me last month whether I regret choosing the school close to home instead of the one far away. I keep meaning to answer honestly. The truth is I don't know yet, and I think anyone who tells you they know is lying. What I can tell you is that the choice I treated as the answer, the obvious peak, stopped being the peak about a year in, and now I'm checking the other end of my life to see what the values are there. Maybe that's a weird way to put it. You'll understand when you take more calculus. Don't decide like I did. I found the one good thing and I stopped looking, and I don't even know yet if the one good thing was the best thing, because I never priced the alternatives. Come visit if you want. The couch is yours.

Eella read it twice. Then she looked at her graph, at the curve rising past its beautiful critical point toward the endpoint she had ignored, and she laughed once, alone, in a way that would have embarrassed her if anyone had heard it.

The next morning she went early to Ms. Becker's room, before the hallway filled. Her teacher was erasing the board, a woman whose silences had a reputation, and Ella laid the quiz on the desk with the graph redrawn beside it, the endpoint marked and its value computed and circled. "I never checked the ends of the interval," Ella said. "So I called a smaller number the maximum. I want to redo it properly."

Ms. Becker looked at the page for a long moment. "Then redo it," she said, and turned back to the board.

In study hall, Everleigh slid into the seat across from her, and Ella pulled out her list of colleges, the ranked one she had never shown anyone, and flattened it on the desk between them. "Tell me about the ones at the bottom," she said. "I keep skipping them."
